claim: ATF6 is one of three endoplasmic reticulum (ER) transmembrane stress sensors that mediate the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6) is one of three endoplasmic reticulum (ER) transmembrane stress sensors that mediate the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the UPR system.

claim: A genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen identified calreticulin (CRT) as a selective repressor of ATF6α signalling.
source: Here, we generated an ATF6α/Inositol-requiring kinase 1 (IRE1) dual UPR reporter CHO-K1 cell line and performed an unbiased genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis screen to systematically profile genetic factors that specifically contribute to ATF6α signalling in the presence and absence of ER stress. The screen identified both anticipated and new candidate genes that regulate ATF6α activation. Among these, calreticulin (CRT), a key ER luminal chaperone, selectively repressed ATF6α signalling
evidence: The screen directly identified CRT as a hit in the ATF6α repressor screen, supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen.

claim: Cells lacking CRT constitutively activated a BiP::sfGFP ATF6α-dependent reporter.
source: Cells lacking CRT constitutively activated a BiP::sfGFP ATF6α-dependent reporter, had higher BiP levels and an increased rate of trafficking and processing of ATF6α.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with CRT-depleted cells.

claim: Cells lacking CRT had higher BiP levels.
source: Cells lacking CRT constitutively activated a BiP::sfGFP ATF6α-dependent reporter, had higher BiP levels and an increased rate of trafficking and processing of ATF6α.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with CRT-depleted cells, shown in immunoblots.

claim: Cells lacking CRT had an increased rate of trafficking and processing of ATF6α.
source: Cells lacking CRT constitutively activated a BiP::sfGFP ATF6α-dependent reporter, had higher BiP levels and an increased rate of trafficking and processing of ATF6α.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with CRT-depleted cells, shown through microscopy and immunoblotting.

claim: Purified CRT interacted with the luminal domain of ATF6α in vitro.
source: Purified CRT interacted with the luminal domain of ATF6α in vitro and the two proteins co-immunoprecipitated from cell lysates.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BioLayer Interferometry (BLI) experiments with purified proteins.

claim: CRT and ATF6α co-immunoprecipitated from cell lysates.
source: Purified CRT interacted with the luminal domain of ATF6α in vitro and the two proteins co-immunoprecipitated from cell lysates.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments from cell lysates.

claim: CRT depletion exposed a negative feedback loop implicating ATF6α in repressing IRE1 activity basally.
source: CRT depletion exposed a negative feedback loop implicating ATF6α in repressing IRE1 activity basally and overexpression of CRT reversed this repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CRT-depleted cells show reduced IRE1 activity, which is consistent with increased ATF6α activity.

claim: Overexpression of CRT reversed the repression of IRE1 activity.
source: CRT depletion exposed a negative feedback loop implicating ATF6α in repressing IRE1 activity basally and overexpression of CRT reversed this repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments where CRT was overexpressed in CRT-depleted cells.

claim: CRT serves as an ER repressor of ATF6α to selectively regulate one arm of the UPR.
source: Our findings indicate that CRT, beyond its known role as a chaperone, also serves as an ER repressor of ATF6α to selectively regulate one arm of the UPR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing CRT's specific effect on ATF6α but not IRE1 or PERK.

claim: The UPR is coordinated by three known ER stress transducers: inositol-requiring kinase 1 (IRE1), protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), and activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6).
source: The UPR is coordinated by three known ER stress transducers: inositol-requiring kinase 1 (IRE1), protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), and activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6) (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ATF6 mediates much of the ER-stress-induced changes in gene expression observed in vertebrates.
source: even though ATF6 mediates much of the ER-stress-induced changes in gene expression observed in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ATF6's role in the UPR.

claim: ATF6 is specialised in the regulation of quality control proteins in the ER.
source: Thus, ATF6 is specialised in the regulation of quality control proteins in the ER (Adachi et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Complete loss of ATF6 impairs survival upon ER stress in cellular and animal models.
source: and complete loss of ATF6 impairs survival upon ER stress in cellular and animal models (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ATF6 is a type II transmembrane ER glycoprotein containing an N-terminal portion comprising its basic leucine zipper (b-ZIP), DNA-binding and transactivation domains and a C-terminal ER luminal domain (LD) that senses stress and regulates ATF6α activity.
source: ATF6 is a type II transmembrane ER glycoprotein containing an N-terminal portion comprising its basic leucine zipper (b-ZIP), DNA-binding and transactivation domains and a C-terminal ER luminal domain (LD) that senses stress and regulates ATF6α activity .
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of ATF6, which is established knowledge.

claim: Vertebrates have two isoforms of ATF6: ATF6α and ATF6β.
source: Vertebrates have two isoforms: ATF6α and ATF6β.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF6 isoforms.

claim: The ATF6α isoform dominates the regulation of UPR target genes in mammalian cells.
source: The ATF6α isoform dominates the regulation of UPR target genes in mammalian cells and is the focus of this study.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relative importance of ATF6α.

claim: ATF6 translocates from the ER to the Golgi upon UPR activation.
source: Unlike IRE1 and PERK, which remain in the ER after UPR activation, ATF6 translocates from the ER to the Golgi
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF6 activation mechanism.

claim: ATF6 is sequentially cleaved by site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases in the Golgi.
source: where it is sequentially cleaved by two serine protease, site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases (Haze et al., 1999)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: S1P and S2P cleavage releases the soluble active N-cytosolic domain (N-ATF6α) of ATF6.
source: to release its soluble active N-cytosolic domain (N-ATF6α) that is further translocated into the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF6 processing.

claim: N-ATF6α acts as a potent but short-lived transcription factor.
source: There, N-ATF6α acts as a potent but short-live transcription factor (George et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: N-ATF6α binds ER stress response elements (ERSE-I and -II) in the promoter regions of UPR target genes in complex with the general transcription factor NF-Y and YY1.
source: that binds ER stress response elements (ERSE-I and -II) in the promoter regions of UPR target genes in complex with the general transcription factor NF-Y and YY1 to upregulate the expression of a large number of ER chaperones (Li et al., 2000; Yoshida et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The gene encoding the ER Hsp70 chaperone BiP (GRP78) is an important ATF6α target.
source: Among those, the gene encoding the ER Hsp70 chaperone BiP (GRP78) has been well documented as an important ATF6α target (Adachi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It has been proposed that ATF6α is retained in the ER by its association with BiP.
source: At ER level, it has been proposed that ATF6α is retained by its association with BiP (Shen et al., 2002)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: Redox regulation has been proposed to keep ATF6α in the ER as a mixture of monomeric and multimeric disulphide-linked forms.
source: Redox regulation has also been proposed to keep ATF6α in the ER as a mixture of monomeric and multimeric disulphide-linked forms (Nadanaka et al., 2007)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: Upon ER stress, ATF6α disulphide-linked forms are reduced by protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) family members (such as ERp18 or PDIA5), promoting the transit of a reduced monomeric ATF6α population.
source: that upon ER stress are reduced by protein disulphide isomerase (PDI) family members (such as ERp18 or PDIA5), promoting the transit of a reduced monomeric ATF6α population (Higa et al., 2014; Oka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: COPII-coated vesicles have been implicated in the trafficking of ATF6α.
source: The Coat Protein Complex II (COPII)-coated vesicles have been implicated in the trafficking of ATF6α (Schindler and Schekman, 2009; Lynch et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ATF6α_LD's N-glycosylation state has been proposed to influence its ER trafficking.
source: and the ATF6α_LD's N-glycosylation state has also been proposed to influence its ER trafficking (Hong et al., 2004)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: A key step of ATF6α activation occurs in the Golgi, the site of proteolytic processing.
source: Furthermore, it is widely recognised that a key step of ATF6α activation occurs in the Golgi, the site of proteolytic processing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF6α activation.

claim: Cells lacking S2P are unable to trigger BiP transcription in response to ER stress.
source: This is reflected in the inability of cells lacking S2P to trigger BiP transcription in response to ER stress (Ye et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ATF6α signalling involves crosstalk with the IRE1 pathway.
source: ATF6α signalling also involves crosstalk with the IRE1 pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UPR signalling.

claim: N-ATF6α directly heterodimerises with XBP1s, the active, spliced form.
source: This is partly mediated by direct heterodimerisation of N-ATF6α with XBP1s, the active, spliced form (Yamamoto et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: XBP1 and IRE1 genes are transcriptional targets of activated ATF6α.
source: (1) XBP1 and IRE1 genes are transcriptional targets of activated ATF6α (Yoshida et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: XBP1s and IRE1 have some different target genes.
source: (2) XBP1s and IRE1 have some different target genes (Shoulders et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ATF6α activity can repress IRE1 signalling.
source: (3) ATF6α activity can also repress IRE1 signalling (Walter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The transcriptional activation of BiP in vertebrates is predominantly governed by ATF6α.
source: In vertebrates, the transcriptional activation of BiP is predominantly governed by ATF6α (Adachi et al., 2008; Adamson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Treatment of XC45-6S cells with ER stress-inducing agents such as tunicamycin, 2-deoxy-D-glucose, or thapsigargin revealed time-dependent activation of both UPR arms with a broad dynamic range.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of these ATF6α/IRE1 dual UPR reporter cells (referred as XC45-6S) treated with ER stress-inducing agents such as tunicamycin (which inhibits N-glycosylation), 2-deoxy-D-glucose (which inhibits glycolysis), or thapsigargin (which depletes ER calcium), revealed time-dependent activation of both UPR arms with a broad dynamic range (Figure 1A, top panel, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The introduction of the reporter systems did not affect basal BiP protein levels when compared with plain CHO-K1 cells.
source: Additionally, the introduction of the reporter systems did not affect basal BiP protein levels when compared with plain CHO-K1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Disruption of endogenous cgATF6α in XC45-6S cells by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing abolished the responsiveness of the BiP::sfGFP reporter to ER stress.
source: Disruption of endogenous cgATF6α in XC45-6S cells by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing abolished the responsiveness of the BiP::sfGFP reporter to ER stress and derepressed IRE1 signalling, both basally and in response to ER stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data in Figure 1A, lower panel.

claim: Disruption of endogenous cgATF6α in XC45-6S cells derepressed IRE1 signalling, both basally and in response to ER stress.
source: Disruption of endogenous cgATF6α in XC45-6S cells by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing abolished the responsiveness of the BiP::sfGFP reporter to ER stress and derepressed IRE1 signalling, both basally and in response to ER stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data in Figure 1A, lower panel.

claim: Ceapin-A7 effectively blocked the activation of the ATF6α fluorescent reporter.
source: Ceapin-A7 effectively blocked the activation of the ATF6α fluorescent reporter, whereas the S1P inhibitor partially attenuated the BiP::sfGFP signal in stressed cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The S1P inhibitor partially attenuated the BiP::sfGFP signal in stressed cells.
source: Ceapin-A7 effectively blocked the activation of the ATF6α fluorescent reporter, whereas the S1P inhibitor partially attenuated the BiP::sfGFP signal in stressed cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The selective IRE1 inhibitor 4μ8C did not affect the ATF6α-dependent BiP::sfGFP reporter under ER stress conditions.
source: The selective IRE1 inhibitor 4μ8C (Cross et al., 2012) did not affect the ATF6α-dependent BiP::sfGFP reporter under ER stress conditions, but blocked the IRE1-dependent XBP1s::mCherry reporter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The selective IRE1 inhibitor 4μ8C blocked the IRE1-dependent XBP1s::mCherry reporter.
source: The selective IRE1 inhibitor 4μ8C (Cross et al., 2012) did not affect the ATF6α-dependent BiP::sfGFP reporter under ER stress conditions, but blocked the IRE1-dependent XBP1s::mCherry reporter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The screen identified S1P and S2P proteases (encoded by the MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 genes) as the two most enriched genes in the ATF6α activator screen.
source: MAGeCK-based analysis of sgRNAs enriched in cells with attenuated ATF6α signalling and intact activity of the IRE1 reporter, revealed that those targeting S1P and S2P proteases (encoding by the MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 genes) were the two most enriched genes (Figure 1C), validating the experimental methodology.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the screen data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) cluster analysis of the 100 most significantly enriched targeted genes in the ATF6α activator screen revealed up to 19 enriched pathways.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) cluster analysis of the 100 most significantly enriched targeted genes revealed up to 19 enriched pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated through GO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: All six sgRNAs targeting FURIN were enriched in the BiP:sfGFPlow cells in the ATF6α activator screen.
source: All six sgRNAs targeting FURIN were enriched in the BiP:sfGFPlow cells, a level of enrichment similar to that observed to the established ATF6α regulators MBTPS1 (S1P) and MBTPS2 (S2P) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Pools of FURIN-targeted cells and an individual FURIN∆ clone had diminished responsiveness of BiP:sfGFP to ER stress.
source: The genotype–phenotype relationship suggested by the screen was also observed upon targeting FURIN in ATF6α/IRE1 dual reporter cells, as both pools of targeted cells and an individual clone had diminished responsiveness of BiP:sfGFP to ER stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The S1P inhibitor more effectively attenuated the BiP::sfGFP reporter in FURIN∆ cells compared to wild-type (WT) cells.
source: Furthermore, the S1P inhibitor more effectively attenuated the BiP::sfGFP reporter in FURIN∆ cells compared to wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, right panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claim: ATF6α_LD expressed and purified from mammalian cells failed to serve as a substrate for FURIN in vitro.
source: However, ATF6α_LD expressed and purified from mammalian cells, failed to serve as a substrate for FURIN in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), suggesting instead that FURIN's role in regulating ATF6α signalling is indirect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro cleavage assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: GO analysis of the 100 most significantly enriched genes in the ATF6α repressor screen established an interconnected network highlighting signalling processes including the calreticulin (CRT)/calnexin (CNX) cycle, N-glycan biosynthesis, ERAD and COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic.
source: GO analysis of the 100 most significantly enriched genes established an interconnected network highlighting signalling processes including the calreticulin (CRT)/calnexin (CNX) cycle, N-glycan biosynthesis, ERAD and COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GO analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Five out of six sgRNAs targeting CRT showed significant enrichment during the selection process in the ATF6α repressor screen.
source: This observation was further supported by the fact that sgRNAs targeting CNX were not enriched, whereas five out of six sgRNAs targeting CRT showed significant enrichment during the selection process (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the screen data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: sgRNAs targeting CNX were not enriched in the ATF6α repressor screen.
source: This observation was further supported by the fact that sgRNAs targeting CNX were not enriched, whereas five out of six sgRNAs targeting CRT showed significant enrichment during the selection process (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the screen data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CRT-targeted cells exhibited large populations of BiP::sfGFPhigh; XBP1s::mCherrylow cells.
source: CRT-targeted cells exhibited large populations of BiP::sfGFPhigh; XBP1s::mCherrylow cells, mirroring the results of the initial screen.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: Targeting CRT repressed the IRE1 reporter basally.
source: Targeting CRT repressed the IRE1 reporter basally and left little room for further induction of the ATF6α reporter upon ER stress (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Targeting CRT left little room for further induction of the ATF6α reporter upon ER stress.
source: Targeting CRT repressed the IRE1 reporter basally and left little room for further induction of the ATF6α reporter upon ER stress (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Derepression of the ATF6α reporter in CRT∆ clones correlated with a slight increase in BiP protein levels.
source: Derepression of the ATF6α reporter in CRT∆ clones correlated with a slight increase in BiP protein levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Depletion of CNX had no impact on the BiP::sfGFP reporter.
source: In contrast, depletion of CNX had no impact on the BiP::sfGFP reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), consistent with the findings of the screen.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and 2C.

claim: ATF6α inactivation in CRT∆ cells restored BiP::sfGFP reporter to its low baseline levels.
source: ATF6α inactivation restored BiP::sfGFP reporter to its low baseline levels and derepressed the IRE1 reporter to levels observed in XC45-6S parental cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ATF6α inactivation in CRT∆ cells derepressed the IRE1 reporter to levels observed in XC45-6S parental cells.
source: ATF6α inactivation restored BiP::sfGFP reporter to its low baseline levels and derepressed the IRE1 reporter to levels observed in XC45-6S parental cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Exposure to dithiothreitol (DTT) increased the Golgi pool of GFP-ATF6α_LDS1P,S2Pmut at the expense of the ER pool.
source: Exposure to the rapidly acting ER stress-inducing agent dithiothreitol (DTT), increased the Golgi pool at the expense of the ER pool (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Compared to parental cells, GFP-ATF6α_LDS1P,S2Pmut showed significantly more Golgi co-localisation in CRT∆ cells under basal conditions.
source: Compared to parental cells, GFP-ATF6α_LDS1P,S2Pmut showed significantly more Golgi co-localisation in CRT∆ cells under basal conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 2K-CRT∆ clonal cells exhibited elevated levels of the processed N-ATF6α form under both basal and stress-induced conditions.
source: 2K-CRT∆ clonal cells exhibited elevated levels of the processed N-ATF6α form under both basal and stress-induced conditions (Figure 3B.1,B.2)
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.1 and 3B.2.

claim: Elevated levels of the processed N-ATF6α form in 2K-CRT∆ cells correlated with a higher nuclear mGL-ATF6α signal observed by live cell microscopy.
source: that correlated with a higher nuclear mGL-ATF6α signal observed by live cell microscopy (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live cell microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Under basal conditions, ATF6α predominantly existed as a high mobility monomer in both 2K-parental and 2K-CRT∆ cells.
source: Under basal conditions, ATF6α predominantly existed as a high mobility monomer in both 2K-parental and 2K-CRT∆ cells, with the appearance of an even faster-migrating processed N-ATF6α form in 2K-CRT∆ cells, consistent with the findings presented in Figure 3B.
evidence: This is demonstrated through non-reducing SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ER stress (induced by 2DG) was associated with appearance of a low-mobility band consistent with a disulfide-stabilised dimer, and a concomitant decrease in the ATF6α monomer intensity in 2K-parental cells.
source: ER stress (induced by 2DG) was associated with appearance of a low-mobility band consistent with a disulfide-stabilised dimer, and a concomitant decrease in the ATF6α monomer intensity in 2K-parental cells, as previously reported (Oka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is demonstrated through non-reducing SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and supported by a citation.

claim: Under stress conditions, the monomer levels in 2K-CRT∆ cells remained largely unchanged, indicating a higher monomer-to-dimer ratio compared to parental cells.
source: Interestingly, under stress conditions, the monomer levels in 2K-CRT∆ cells remained largely unchanged, indicating a higher monomer-to-dimer ratio compared to parental cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through non-reducing SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BLI showed reversible binding of CRT to ATF6α_LDWT that was characterised by slow association (kon) and dissociation (koff) rates.
source: BLI showed reversible binding of CRT to ATF6α_LDWT that was characterised by slow association (kon) and dissociation (koff) rates (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BLI data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The association and dissociation phases of CRT binding to ATF6α_LDWT were fitted to a single exponential association-dissociation model, yielding a KD within the range of 1 µM.
source: Both the association and dissociation phases were fitted to a single exponential association-dissociation model, yielding a KD within the range of 1 µM, a concentration that was consisted with the estimated CRT concentration in the ER of CHO-K1 cells obtained through quantitative immunoblotting (~7 µM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BLI data shown in Figure 4B and quantitative immunoblotting shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar interactions to those observed with ATF6α_LDWT were also observed with ATF6α_LD∆Gly and ATF6α_LD∆C.
source: Similar interactions were also observed with ATF6α_LD∆Gly and ATF6α_LD∆C.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BLI data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both ATF6α_LDWT and, to a lesser extent, ATF6α_LD∆Gly immunoprecipitated endogenous CRT from HEK293T cells.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation results showed that both ATF6α_LDWT and, to a lesser extent, ATF6α_LD∆Gly immunoprecipitated endogenous CRT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GFP-ATF6_LD∆Gly was expressed at lower levels than ATF6α_LDWT in HEK293T cells.
source: Re-probing the blot with an anti-GFP antibody revealed that GFP-ATF6_LD∆Gly was expressed at lower levels than ATF6α_LDWT (Figure 4C), potentially accounting for the reduced recovery of CRT in complex with ATF6α_LD∆Gly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Unlike the ATF6α_LDWT, neither the ATF6α_LD∆Gly nor the ATF6α_LD∆C repair templates fully restored BiP::sfGFP responsiveness to stress.
source: Unlike the ATF6α_LDWT, neither the ATF6α_LD∆Gly nor the ATF6α_LD∆C repair templates fully restored BiP::sfGFP responsiveness to stress (Figure 5B, top panel)
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ATF6α_LD∆C knock-in cells exhibited basal activation of the IRE1 reporter comparable to levels observed in the ATF6α∆ parent.
source: Notably, whereas ATF6α_LD∆C knock-in cells exhibited basal activation of the IRE1 reporter comparable to levels observed in the ATF6α∆ parent (Figure 5B, lower panel)
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The IRE1 reporter signal in the ATF6α_LD∆Gly knock-in cells shifted to that observed in WT cells.
source: the IRE1 reporter signal in the ATF6α_LD∆Gly knock-in cells shifted to that observed in WT cells, suggesting that ∆Gly allele retained some functionality.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of CRTWT restored basal levels of both BiP::sfGFP and XBP1s:mCherry reporters in CRT∆ cells.
source: Expression of CRTWT restored basal levels of both BiP::sfGFP and XBP1s:mCherry reporters in CRT∆ cells (Figure 6A, purple panels and Figure 6B), confirming the repressive role of CRT on ATF6α.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Expression of the double CRTY92A,W244A mutant failed to rescue the CRT∆ phenotype.
source: In contrast, expression of the double CRTY92A,W244A mutant failed to rescue the CRT∆ phenotype (Figure 6A, green panels and Figure 6B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: CRTY92A, selectively incapable of glycan binding, retained some ability to repress BiP::sfGFP and modestly rescued the CRT∆ phenotype.
source: whereas CRTY92A, selectively incapable of glycan binding, retained some ability to repress BiP::sfGFP and modestly rescuing the CRT∆ phenotype (Figure 6A, orange panels and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: CRTWT and CRTY92A proteins were expressed similarly in CHO-K1 cells.
source: However, CRTWT and CRTY92A proteins were expressed similarly (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Under basal conditions, unspliced XBP1 mRNA levels (XBP1u) were significantly higher in CRT∆ clones compared to parental cells.
source: Under basal conditions, unspliced mRNA levels (XBP1u) were significantly higher in CRT∆ clones (Figure 7A, left bar graph), consistent with the role of NATF6α in the transcriptional activation of XBP1 (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A, and supported by a citation.

claim: Compared to parental cells, CRT∆ cells exhibited a smaller fraction of spliced XBP1 mRNA (XBP1s).
source: In addition, compared to parental cells, CRT∆ cells exhibited a smaller fraction of spliced XBP1 mRNA (XBP1s) (Figure 7A, right bar graph), consistent with the lower IRE1 activity measured by a XBP1s::mCherry reporter.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CRT∆ cells exhibited lower levels of stress-induced phosphorylation of their endogenous IRE1 protein.
source: Accordingly, CRT∆ cells exhibited lower levels of stress-induced phosphorylation of their endogenous IRE1 protein and slightly reduced total IRE1 levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CRT∆ cells had slightly reduced total IRE1 levels.
source: Accordingly, CRT∆ cells exhibited lower levels of stress-induced phosphorylation of their endogenous IRE1 protein and slightly reduced total IRE1 levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the presence of ER stress, all genotypes (parental and CRT∆) exhibited a comparable increase in XBP1s.
source: However, the defect in IRE1 activity in CRT-depleted cells was partial, as in the presence of ER stress, all genotypes exhibited a comparable increase in XBP1s (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A connection between CRT and ATF6α was proposed previously based on an interaction between overexpressed proteins.
